en.content:
The sharp jump in fuel surcharges announced by Taiwanese carriers this week, driven by a spike in oil prices after the escalation of conflict in the Middle East, is a reminder that distant geopolitics can have immediate effects on Hong Kong’s pocketbooks and businesses. For a city that depends on aviation for tourism, trade and frequent personal travel, a 157 percent increase in surcharges on international flights is not an abstract number: it will translate into higher fares, tighter household budgets and reduced demand for discretionary travel just as the sector is trying to recover from pandemic disruptions.

It is also worth recognising why airlines take such measures. Fuel is a major variable cost for carriers and rapid oil-price movements force airlines either to absorb losses or pass costs to passengers. Hedging practices, fleet efficiency and route economics determine how much pain an individual airline can shoulder. For Hong Kong — home to a high-density blend of long-haul and regional services — the economic ripple effects will be felt beyond airfares, extending to hospitality, retail and the MICE sectors that underpin jobs and small businesses.

Policy responses should be pragmatic and proportionate. Authorities in Hong Kong can play a constructive role by ensuring transparent disclosure of fare components so consumers understand what they are paying for, monitoring for unfair practices, and engaging with carriers to keep essential connectivity affordable. At the same time, industry and regulators should accelerate structural measures that reduce vulnerability to oil shocks: improved fuel-efficiency standards, investment in newer aircraft, smarter route planning, prudent hedging strategies and long-term commitment to sustainable aviation fuels and electrification where feasible.

Finally, while the root causes of such market volatility lie beyond Hong Kong’s immediate control, this episode underlines the importance of resilience. The government, business and civil society should work together to shield households and the economy from short-term shocks, while advancing the longer-term transitions that will make Hong Kong’s transport and trade networks less exposed to the vagaries of global geopolitics. In the near term, clear communication, coordinated contingency planning and sensible support for affected sectors will best preserve the city’s connectivity and competitiveness.

zh.content:
中東衝突令國際油價急升，台灣航空在周二宣布把國際航班燃油附加費加幅達157%，香港旅客同本地航空業都會感受到呢股漲價壓力。燃油成本係航空公司最大開支之一，面對突如其來嘅外部衝擊，企業選擇把成本轉嫁畀乘客，係市場上常見嘅短期反應；但香港作為一個國際航空樞紐，呢啲漲幅無可避免會推高旅遊成本，影響旅客意欲同旅遊業復甦嘅節奏。

政府角色應係穩定而非對抗：要做到資訊透明、監察市場運作，避免不合理嘅價格操控，並向市民解釋燃油附加費嘅成分同計算方法，減少恐慌性情緒。對航空公司而言，除咗短期調整收費外，亦應考慮透過燃料對沖、提升燃油效率、優化航線同承載率等手段分擔風險。政府可以適時提供政策協調，例如協助旅遊業作臨時支援，鼓勵多元化市場推廣，減低對單一客源或季節性旅遊旺季嘅依賴。

長遠睇，呢次事件提醒香港要加強能源同經濟抗風險能力。除咗支持航空同旅遊業恢復外，亦應推動更廣泛嘅供應鏈彈性、加快轉向更高能效同低碳的運輸技術，從而減少未來類似國際衝突對本地生活嘅直接衝擊。政府、企業同市民三方面合作，既要穩住短期民生與市道，亦要着手長遠策略，維持香港作為穩定、可靠嘅國際交通與旅遊中心地位。

China Airlines plane. File photo: Jeffry Surianto, via Pexels.



Surcharges on short-haul flights will increase by US$27.50 to US$45 and US$71.50 to US$117 for longer flights, the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) and transportation ministry said on Wednesday.
